questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted inline citations to the specific chart text behind each AI-generated suggestion in the prior authorization drafts. They emphasized the need to "show your work," meaning they wanted transparency into the source of each claim in the draft justifications [1]. This requirement was identified as a durable need across both the April 2025 (v1) and November 2025 (v2) testing rounds [1]. In v2, the citations were implemented as links to specific chart-text spans rather than section headers, allowing nurses to verify the accuracy of the AI-generated content [2]. Three out of four participants in the v2 testing clicked into at least one citation to verify before accepting, and they described this process as appropriately fast and not a source of friction [3]. A returning participant from v1, the Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor), stated, "This is what I wanted in April. It shows its work, it got the codes right..." [4].

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization Drafting — Service Topology (v2)
sources.excerpt: Encounter chart -> Chart-Data Service (pulls diagnosis/treatment history) -> Drafting Model (generates justification text + inline citations back to specific chart spans) -> Payer-Rules Lookup (validates against current, not cached, diagnosis codes — the fix that closed the v1 data-freshness bug) -> UM Review Queue (nurse accepts/edits/rejects) -> Submission Service. Citation links resolve to specific chart-text spans rather than section headers, which is why nurses could meaningfully check at least one citation before accepting in v2.

questions.question: How were sound-alike medication names handled?

seeded.answer:
Initially, sound-alike medication names were treated as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them [1]. Before GA, medication dosage errors dropped from 3/5 sessions (v0.1) to 1/5 (v0.2), but sound-alike medication names remained a tracked issue [2].

A usability test was conducted with 6 participants (Physicians and Nurse Practitioners) using 6 simulated encounters with known sound-alike pairs, such as hydralazine/hydroxyzine and clonidine/Klonopin [3]. The test explored a distinct flag for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline [1].

The concept test found that 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized the flag as different from generic low confidence, but 2 of 6 participants expressed over-trust in unflagged medication lines [4]. Based on this, a dedicated sound-alike-medication flag was developed with a small amber pill-shaped badge placed inline after the medication name, with a short on-hover/on-tap label prompting verification [5].

This is now the official pre-AI baseline for measuring Compass AI's impact at 6 and 12 months post-GA. Caveat: the September survey mentioned the AI initiative explicitly in its framing, while the February survey didn't — any comparison between the two datasets needs to account for that framing difference, not treat them as a clean before/after.

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

seeded.answer: Staff awareness of Compass AI initiatives varied significantly between clinical and non-clinical staff. Specifically, 71% of clinical staff reported being aware of the initiatives, while only 34% of non-clinical staff were aware, indicating a notable awareness gap [1]. This suggests that internal communications have primarily focused on clinical staff and may need to be broadened to include non-clinical staff, especially as non-clinical rollouts such as scheduling proceed [2].
